title: Recommendations and Plain-Language Translation
summary: Learn to turn analytical findings into concrete recommendations using the 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern, and to rewrite technical results in plain language by glossing specialist terms and replacing formal words with simpler ones.

steps.title: From finding to action: the 'because X, recommend Y' pattern
steps.lede: A finding that sits in a report, unconnected to any suggested action, may not help the manager who needs to decide something.

blocks.text: Having found that Lagos delivery times rose, the next step is turning that finding into something the operations manager can act on. The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon — a finding that sits in a report, unconnected to any suggested action, may not do much for the manager who needs to decide something.

The pattern is: 'because we found X, we recommend Y.' For example: '...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program.' Following that same pattern for the delivery finding: 'because the average Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes this month, we recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route.' The finding directly justifies the action.

steps.title: Spotting a data-grounded recommendation
steps.lede: Which of the following best follows the 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern for a finding that average Kano delivery times rose from 21 to 22.5 minutes?

public.prompt: Average Kano delivery times rose from 21.0 to 22.5 minutes between Month 1 and Month 2. Which option best follows the 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern?

options.text: Because average Kano delivery times rose from 21.0 to 22.5 minutes, we recommend adding a courier to the Kano route.
We recommend adding a courier to the Kano route to improve performance.
Because delivery times have been increasing, we recommend reviewing operations.
We should add a courier to the Kano route because that is what the operations manager wants.

opt_correct.message: Correct. This recommendation names the specific finding (21.0 to 22.5 minutes) and connects it directly to a concrete action (adding a courier) — exactly the 'because X, we recommend Y' pattern.

opt_no_finding.message: Not quite. This recommendation states an action but gives no data finding to justify it. A data-driven recommendation must cite the specific finding that supports the action.

opt_vague.message: Not quite. 'Delivery times have been increasing' is too vague — it does not cite the specific numbers. A data-driven recommendation names the precise finding.

opt_reversed.message: Not quite. This justifies the recommendation by what the manager wants, not by a data finding. The 'because X' part must be a data result, not a stakeholder preference.

correct.message: Correct. A data-driven recommendation names the specific finding and connects it to a concrete action.

incorrect.message: Remember: the recommendation must cite the specific data finding ('because we found X') and connect it to a concrete action ('we recommend Y').

hints: Which option actually names a specific number from the data as the reason for the recommendation?
The 'because' clause must be a data result — a specific finding, not a general observation or a stakeholder preference.

steps.title: Write a data-grounded recommendation
steps.lede: Review a set of QuickShip delivery findings. Select the columns and values that justify a recommendation, then connect them to a concrete suggested action.

public.intro: The table shows average delivery times and order volumes for three cities across two months. Select the cells that provide the strongest data justification for a recommendation to add a courier to the Lagos route.

tasks.prompt: Select the cell showing Lagos's average delivery time in Month 1 — the baseline before the increase.
Select the cell showing Lagos's average delivery time in Month 2 — the value that reveals the problem.

task_baseline_value.correct: Correct. 22.0 minutes is the Lagos baseline in Month 1 — the starting point that makes the Month 2 increase meaningful.
task_baseline_value.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the Lagos row in Month 1 and select the average delivery time — that is the baseline before the increase.

task_current_value.correct: Correct. 30.0 minutes in Month 2 is the finding that justifies the recommendation — the rise from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes is the 'because X' in 'because we found X, we recommend Y'.
task_current_value.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the Lagos row in Month 2 and select the average delivery time — that is the value that reveals the problem.

correct.message: Well done. The rise from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes in Lagos is the specific finding that justifies a recommendation — 'because average Lagos delivery times rose from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes, we recommend adding a courier to the Lagos route.'

incorrect.message: Look for the Lagos rows and select the average delivery time values that show the change between months.

hints: A data-driven recommendation needs a specific 'before' and 'after' value — which city shows the largest change?
Find the Lagos rows and compare the average delivery times across the two months.

steps.title: Replacing jargon and formal words
steps.lede: An analysis can accumulate technical terms that a non-technical manager won't follow. Two rules keep your writing clear.

blocks.text: Specialist terms can be used where needed — they are not always jargon — but explain them in plain English the first time they appear. If 'the average delivery time' needs to be called out as a mean for precision, saying 'the average (mean) delivery time' once keeps both the plain and the technical reader covered.

Formal or long words should be avoided when an easy or short one will do — for example 'buy' instead of 'purchase', 'help' instead of 'assist', 'about' instead of 'approximately'. Jargon and buzzwords should also be avoided because they are often vague and can be misinterpreted. 'Delivery times got worse this month' reads more plainly than 'delivery time performance exhibited negative variance this period.'

nodes.label: Technical: 'The mean delivery time exhibited a statistically significant increase of approximately 8 minutes, suggesting negative operational variance in the Lagos route.'

before.alt_text: A technically-worded sentence using 'mean', 'statistically significant', 'approximately', and 'negative operational variance'.

nodes.label: Plain: 'The average (mean) delivery time rose by about 8 minutes in Lagos this month — deliveries got slower.'

after.alt_text: The plain-language rewrite: 'mean' is glossed as 'average (mean)', 'approximately' becomes 'about', and 'negative operational variance' becomes 'got slower'.

blocks.change_summary: 'approximately' → 'about'; 'exhibited a statistically significant increase' → 'rose'; 'negative operational variance' → 'got slower'; 'mean' glossed as 'average (mean)' on first use.

steps.title: Replacing a formal word with a simpler one
steps.lede: Which word best replaces 'utilise' in the sentence: 'We should utilise the new courier route to reduce delivery times'?

public.prompt: Which word best replaces 'utilise' in the sentence: 'We should utilise the new courier route to reduce delivery times'?

opt_use.message: Correct. 'Use' is the short, everyday word that replaces the formal 'utilise' — plain language prefers the simpler equivalent.

opt_employ.message: Not quite. 'Employ' is also a formal word — it is no simpler than 'utilise'. Plain language calls for the shortest, most everyday word: 'use'.

opt_leverage.message: Not quite. 'Leverage' is a buzzword that is often vague and can be misinterpreted. Plain language avoids jargon and buzzwords; 'use' is the clear, simple choice.

opt_implement.message: Not quite. 'Implement' is a formal word that is longer and less everyday than 'use'. Plain language prefers the short, simple equivalent.

correct.message: Correct. 'Use' is the short, everyday word that replaces the formal 'utilise' — exactly the kind of substitution plain language calls for.

incorrect.message: Remember: plain language replaces formal or long words with short, everyday equivalents. 'Utilise' → 'use' is a classic example.

hints: Which of the options is the shortest, most everyday word for the same action?
Plain language avoids formal words like 'utilise', 'employ', and buzzwords like 'leverage' — which option is the simplest?

steps.title: Match technical results to their plain-language rewrites
steps.lede: Each technical result below has one plain-language rewrite that correctly applies the two rules: specialist terms glossed on first use, and formal words replaced with simpler equivalents. Match them.

public.prompt: Each sentence below is a plain-language rewrite of a technical result. Classify each rewrite by which plain-language rule it applies: Rule 1 — specialist terms are glossed on first use; Rule 2 — formal or long words are replaced with simpler equivalents.

buckets.label: Rule 1 only — specialist term glossed in plain English
Rule 2 only — formal word replaced with a simpler one

items.text: The average (mean) Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes.
Lagos delivery times got worse this month.
The average (mean) delivery time — how long each order takes from dispatch to doorstep — rose by 8 minutes, so we recommend adding a courier.
Delivery time performance exhibited negative variance this period.

item_gloss_only.message: Correct. 'The average (mean)' glosses the specialist term 'mean' in plain English on first use — Rule 1. No formal words are replaced here, so only Rule 1 applies.

item_replace_only.message: Correct. 'Got worse' replaces the formal phrase 'exhibited negative variance' with a short, everyday equivalent — Rule 2. No specialist term is glossed, so only Rule 2 applies.

item_both.message: Correct. 'The average (mean)' glosses the specialist term (Rule 1), and the sentence replaces formal alternatives with plain words like 'rose' instead of 'increased' and 'recommend' instead of 'advise' (Rule 2). Both rules are applied.

item_trap.message: This sentence applies neither rule. 'Exhibited' is a formal word that should be replaced with 'showed' or 'got worse' (Rule 2 not applied), and 'negative variance' is jargon that is not glossed (Rule 1 not applied). This is the kind of technical sentence that needs to be rewritten.

correct.message: Well done. You correctly identified which plain-language rule each rewrite applies — and spotted the sentence that applies neither rule.

incorrect.message: Review the two rules: Rule 1 glosses specialist terms on first use; Rule 2 replaces formal or long words with simpler equivalents. Which rule does each rewrite apply?

hints: Look for parenthetical glosses like '(mean)' — that is Rule 1 in action. Look for short, everyday words replacing formal ones — that is Rule 2.
One sentence applies neither rule — it still uses formal language and unexplained jargon. Which one is it?

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Two moves that turn analysis into communication a stakeholder can act on.

blocks.text: Analytical value is only realized when findings lead to action. The 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern connects a specific finding directly to a concrete suggested action. Plain-language translation keeps the message accessible: gloss specialist terms on first use, and replace formal or long words with simpler equivalents — 'about' not 'approximately', 'help' not 'assist'.

blocks.text: In the next tile you'll learn how to decide which findings to lead with and which to leave out, so your stakeholder hears the most relevant information first.

remediation_steps.title: Data-grounded vs. ungrounded recommendation: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two recommendations about Lagos delivery times — one grounded in data, one not.

blocks.text: Ungrounded: 'We should add more couriers to Lagos.' No finding is cited — the recommendation floats free of the data. Grounded: 'Because the average Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes this month, we recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route.' The specific finding (22 → 30 minutes) directly justifies the specific action (one more courier). The 'because X, recommend Y' structure makes the link explicit.

remediation_steps.title: Plain language: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: The same finding — one version technical, one plain.

blocks.text: Technical: 'The median (M = 26 min) was below the mean (M = 29.2 min), indicating positive skewness in the delivery-time distribution.' Plain: 'Most deliveries finished in about 26 minutes, but a few very slow orders pulled the average (mean) up to about 29 minutes — the data is skewed right.' Changes: 'M = 26 min' → 'about 26 minutes'; 'positive skewness' → 'skewed right'; 'mean' glossed as 'average (mean)' on first use; 'indicating' → dropped in favour of a plain causal phrase.
